page: Vultr vhp-2c-2gb-amd is an entry-level virtual server within the High Performance lineup, designed for compute tasks with modest memory footprints. It is provisioned on the x86_64 architecture using an AMD EPYC processor clocked at 2.0 GHz. The virtual machine allocates 2 shared vCPUs derived from a single hyperthreaded physical core, accompanied by 32 KB L1 data cache, 0.5 MB L2 cache, and a 16 MB L3 cache segment. It includes 2.0 GB of system memory, matching a 1.0 GB per vCPU ratio, alongside a bundled 60 GB NVMe SSD and one complimentary public IPv4 address. No dedicated hardware GPUs are present.

Benchmark results show a split performance profile. Single-core compute throughput measured via stress-ng scores 3206.39, placing the instance in the top 10 percent of recorded servers. Multi-core stress-ng performance reaches 6339.69, which is in the middle 50 percent. Conversely, aggregate PassMark CPU testing ranks in the lower 25 percent at 5245.37, impacted by lower scores in physics (665.15) and encryption (2633.97). Uncached large-block memory read and write bandwidth register at 41.62 GB/sec and 33.03 GB/sec respectively, whereas PassMark memory and database metrics place in the bottom 10 percent.

Because execution resources rely on a shared-core model and memory is strictly limited to 2.0 GB, resource contention and memory pressure remain key operational tradeoffs. Throughput in static web serving reaches 2.53 GB/sec and Redis SET operations attain 4.07 million operations per second, both lower-tier results. Consequently, the vhp-2c-2gb-amd instance represents a cost-efficient resource tier primarily suitable for non-memory-intensive workloads, including lightweight background processing, low-traffic APIs, small CI/CD runners, and edge orchestration utilities.
description: Vultr vhp-2c-2gb-amd is an entry-tier cloud instance built on the x86_64 AMD EPYC architecture, providing 2 shared vCPUs across 1 physical core, 2.0 GB of RAM, and 60 GB of bundled local NVMe SSD storage. The processor delivers strong single-core compute performance in stress-ng benchmarks, though multi-core and overall PassMark metrics reflect its shared dual-thread configuration. Memory throughput on large uncached blocks is moderate at 41.62 GB/sec read and 33.03 GB/sec write, but total memory allocation limits high-density database and caching tasks, as evidenced by low Redis and web-serving benchmark ratings. Without dedicated GPUs, this instance serves as a cost-efficient computing node for small utilities, development staging, low-volume microservices, and lightweight automation scripts.
